A.explanation: About $10\text{ J}$ is far too small and corresponds to a mass of about $1\text{ kg}$ moving at a few $\text{m s}^{-1}$.

B.explanation: About $100\text{ J}$ is still an order of magnitude too small for a $70\text{ kg}$ adult running at several $\text{m s}^{-1}$.

C.explanation: Using $m \approx 70\text{ kg}$ and $v \approx 5\text{ m s}^{-1}$ gives $E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 \approx 900\text{ J}$, closest to $1000\text{ J}$.

D.explanation: About $10\,000\text{ J}$ is too large and would need an elite sprint speed of about $17\text{ m s}^{-1}$ for a $70\text{ kg}$ man.

hints: Estimate the two missing quantities for a running adult man: a typical mass in $\text{kg}$ of about $60$-$80$ and a steady running speed in $\text{m s}^{-1}$ of about $3$-$6$.
Recall the kinetic energy relation $E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$ in joules, so the speed is squared and has the larger effect on the order of magnitude.
Substitute your estimates, for example $m \approx 70\text{ kg}$ and $v \approx 5\text{ m s}^{-1}$, and compare the result to the powers of ten $10$, $100$, $1000$ and $10\,000\text{ J}$.
walkthrough: No mass or speed is given, so make sensible estimates for a man running in a straight line: take $m \approx 70\text{ kg}$ and $v \approx 5\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
State the governing rule for translational kinetic energy: $E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$.
Substitute the estimates with units: $E_k \approx 0.5 \times 70\text{ kg} \times (5\text{ m s}^{-1})^2$.
Calculate the intermediate result: $(5)^2 = 25$, so $E_k \approx 0.5 \times 70 \times 25 = 875\text{ J} \approx 10^3\text{ J}$, with unit $\text{J} = \text{kg m}^2\text{ s}^{-2}$.
An order-of-magnitude estimate only needs the nearest power of ten, so $875\text{ J}$ is much closer to $1000\text{ J}$ than to $100\text{ J}$ or $10\,000\text{ J}$. This is option C.
